It has been said: from «جَنَبْتُ الفَرَسَ» (I led the horse by my side), as though [he asked] that He lead him away from the side of polytheism by His kindnesses and hidden means."

And {أَن نَّعْبُدَ} is on the omission of the preposition, i.e. «عن أن». Al-Jaḥdarī and ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī read «وأَجْنِبْني» with a disjunctive hamza, from «أَجْنَبَ».

semin-durr:36-36.t:
The pronoun in «إنَّهُنَّ» and «أَضْلَلْنَ» refers back to the idols, because they are a broken plural of a non-rational. His word «مني», i.e. of my followers.

His words: {وَمَنْ عَصَانِي}: a condition; the position of «مَنْ» is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject); the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is {فَإِنَّكَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ}, and the referent pronoun is omitted, i.e. "for him".

semin-durr:37-37.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {مِن ذُرِّيَّتِي}: the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) may be omitted, with this prepositional phrase its attribute, i.e. "I have settled some offspring from my offspring". «مِنْ» may also be redundant (zāʾida) according to al-Akhfash.

His words: «بوادٍ», i.e. in a valley, as in «هو بمكة» ("he is in Mecca").

His words: {عِندَ بَيْتِكَ}: it may be an attribute of «وادٍ». Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It may be a badal (substitute) from it", meaning a badal of part from whole, since the valley is more general than the vicinity of the House. There is a reservation about this, in that «عند» is not freely inflected (lā yataṣarraf).

His words: «ليُقِيموا»: this lām may be the lām of command, or the lām of cause. In the latter case there are two views about what it is attached to. One: it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «أَسْكنْتُ», which is apparent, the vocative being parenthetical. The other: it is attached to «اجْنُبْني», i.e. "keep them away from idols so that they may establish", and this is far-fetched.

His words: {أَفْئِدَةً مِّنَ الناس}: the generality read «أفْئِدة», plural of «فُؤاد», like «غُراب/أَغْربة». Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a yāʾ after the hamza. It has been said: this is lengthening (ishbāʿ), as in the saying:
289 - 5-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يُحِبَّك عَظْمٌ في الترابِ تَرِيْبُ
(… a bone lying in the dust will love you.)
i.e. «تَرِب»; and as in the saying:
289 - 6- أعوذُ باللهِ مِنَ العَقْرابِ ... الشائلاتِ عُقدَ الأَذْنابِ
(I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpions that raise the knots of their tails.)
A group attacked this reading and said: lengthening is one of the licences of poetry, so how can it be put in the most eloquent speech? Some claimed that Hishām only read it with the hamza lightened to an in-between sound (bayna bayna), and the transmitter thought it was the addition of a yāʾ after the hamza; he said: "just as it was imagined of Abū ʿAmr's slurring (ikhtilās) in «بارئكم» and «يَأْمُركم» that he gave sukūn." This is nothing, for the transmitters are too eminent for this.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «إفادة» on the pattern of «رِفادة». There are two views on it. First: it is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of «أفاد», like «أقام إقامةً», i.e. possessors of benefit — the people from whom benefit is had. Second: its origin is «وِفادة» (a delegation's coming), the wāw being replaced by a hamza, as in «إشاح» and «إعاء».

Umm al-Haytham read «أَفْوِدَة» with a wāw with kasra. There are two views on it. First: it is the plural of the lightened «فُوَاد»: a hamza with fatḥa preceded by ḍamma is regularly changed into a wāw, as in «جُوَن»; this was done in the singular «فُؤاد», and it was kept as it was in the plural. Second: the author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "It is the plural of «وَفْد»." I say: then the form should have been «أَوْفِدة», with the wāw first — unless it is said that he pluralised «وَفْد» as «أَوْفِدَة» and then transposed it, so its measure is «أَعْفِلَة», like their saying «آرام» for «أرْآم» and its class; except that the plural of faʿl on afʿila is rare, as in «نَجْد/أَنْجدة» and «وَهْي/أَوْهِيَة». Umm al-Haytham is a woman from whom something of the language has been transmitted.

It has been read «آفِدَة» on the pattern of «ضارِبة». It admits two views. First: it is transposed from «أَفئدة», with the hamza put before the fāʾ, then the hamza changed into an alif, so its measure is «أَعْفِلة», like «آرام» for «أرْآم».
Second: it is an active participle of «أَفِد يَأْفَدُ», i.e. to draw near, the meaning being "an approaching group", or "approaching groups".

It has been read «أَفِدَة» without the long vowel [Translator's note: the source writes «آفِدَة» here too, but says "with shortening (bi-l-qaṣr)"], and there are two views on this too. First: it is an active-participle adjective on the pattern faʿil, like «فَرِحَ فهو فَرِح». [Second]: it is lightened from «أَفْئِدة» by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the vowelless letter before it and dropping the hamza.

And «من الناس»: there are two views about «مِنْ». First: it is for the beginning of the extent. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«مِنْ» may be for the beginning of the extent, as when you say 'The heart from me is sick', meaning 'my heart'; as though it were said 'hearts of people'. I only made the muḍāf indefinite in this illustration because «أَفْئدة» is indefinite — since in the verse it is indefinite — so that it comprises some of the hearts." The Shaykh said: "Its being for the extent is not apparent, because we have no verb in which there is a beginning with an extent at which it ends, since it is not valid to make the beginning of the hearts from the people."
Second: it is partitive. In the exegesis: had he not said «من الناس», all people would have made the pilgrimage.

His words: «تَهْوي»: this is the second object of «الجَعْل». The generality read «تَهْوِي» with kasra on the ʿayn, meaning: they hasten and fly with longing to them. The poet said:
289 - 7- وإذا رَمَيْتَ به الفِجاجَ رَأَيْتَه ... يَهْوي مخارمَها هُوِيَّ الأجْدَلِ
(When you launch him into the mountain passes, you see him swooping through their defiles as the falcon swoops.)
Its original is to be made transitive with the lām, as in the saying:
289 - 8- حتى إذا ما هَوَتْ كفُّ الغلامِ لها ... طارَتْ وفي كَفِّه مِنْ ريشِها بِتَكُ
(Until, when the boy's hand swooped at her, she flew off, leaving in his hand plucked tufts of her feathers.)
It was only made transitive with «إلى» because it was made to imply the sense of «تميل» ("to incline"), as in the saying:
289 - 9- تَهْوي إلى مكَّةَ تَبْغي الهدى ... ما مُؤْمِنُ الجِنِّ كأَنْجاسِها
(She hastens to Mecca seeking guidance; the believer among the jinn is not like their unclean ones.)
The Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad and Mujāhid read it with fatḥa on the wāw [«تَهْوَى»]. There are two views on it. First: «إلى» is redundant, i.e. "they love them". Second: it was made to imply the sense of "yearn and incline". The maṣdar of the first [form] is «هُوِيّ», as in the saying:
290 - 0-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يَهْوي مخارِمَها هُوِيَّ الأجْدَل
(… swooping through their defiles as the falcon swoops.)
and that of the second is «هَوَى». Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Their meanings are close, except that «هَوِيَ» — meaning with fatḥa on the wāw [in the imperfect] — is transitive by itself, and it was only made transitive with «إلى» by construal on «تميل»."

Maslama ibn ʿAbd Allāh read «تُهْوَى», with ḍamma on the tāʾ and fatḥa on the wāw, passive, from «أهوى», transferred from the intransitive «هَوِيَ», i.e. they are made to hasten to them.

semin-durr:39-39.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {عَلَى الكبر}: there are two views. First: «على» is in its proper sense of figurative superiority. Second: it means «مع» ("with, despite"), as in the saying:
290 - 1- إنِّي على ما تَرَيْنَ من كِبَري ... أعلمُ مِنْ تُؤْكَلُ الكَتِفَ
(Despite the old age you see in me, I know from where the shoulder is eaten [i.e. I know how to handle affairs].)
Al-Zamakhsharī said this. The position of this prepositional phrase is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the yāʾ in «هَبْ لي».
[Translator's note: the source has «من الباء»; the pronoun in «لي» is the yāʾ, which is evidently meant.]

His words: {لَسَمِيعُ الدعآء}: there are several views. First: faʿīl is an intensive form in construct with its object, the construct arising from an accusative; this is evidence for Sībawayh that faʿīl operates like the active participle, even though he differed from the majority of Basrans and Kufans in this.

Second: the construct does not arise from an accusative; it is only like your saying «هذا ضاربُ زيدٍ أمس» ("this is the one who struck Zayd yesterday"). Third: «سميع» is in construct with its nominative [subject], Allah's prayer being made "hearing" figuratively, what is meant being Allah's hearing — al-Zamakhsharī said this.

The Shaykh said: "It is far-fetched, because it entails its being a ṣifa mushabbaha (adjective resembling the participle) while the adjective is transitive; this only works on the view of al-Fārisī, who allows the ṣifa mushabbaha to be from a transitive verb on condition that ambiguity is avoided, as in «زيد ظالمُ العبيد» ('Zayd whose slaves are unjust') when it is known that he has unjust slaves. Here, however, ambiguity is present, since the apparent sense is that it is the intensive form in construct with the object, not the agent."
I say: ambiguity here too is absent, because the meaning is on figurative attribution as established, so ambiguity is ruled out.

semin-durr:40-40.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {وَمِن ذُرِّيَتِي}: conjoined to the first object of «اجعلني», i.e. "and make some of my offspring establishers of prayer". This prepositional phrase is in reality an attribute of that omitted [object], i.e. "and some from my offspring".

His words: {وَتَقَبَّلْ دُعَآءِ}: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and Warsh read it with the yāʾ kept in continuous reading and dropped in pause; al-Bazzī kept it in both states; and the rest dropped it both in continuous reading and in pause. Some have transmitted its being kept in pause as well.

semin-durr:41-41.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {وَلِوَالِدَيَّ}: the generality read «والِدَيَّ» with an alif after the wāw and a doubled yāʾ. Ibn Jubayr read likewise, except that he gave the yāʾ sukūn, meaning his father alone, as in His words {واغفر لأبي} [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 86].

Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, Muḥammad and Zayd the sons of ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, and Ibn Yaʿmar read «ولولدي» without an alif, the dual of «وَلَد», meaning by the two Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq. Al-Jaḥdarī rejected it on the ground that in the codex of Ubayy it is «ولأبويَّ», which explains the reading of the generality.

It is related from Ibn Yaʿmar that he read «ولِوُلْدي» with ḍamma on the wāw and sukūn on the yāʾ. There are two interpretations of it. One: it is the plural of «وَلَد», like «أُسْد» from «أَسَد». The other: it is a dialectal variant of «الوَلَد», like «الحُزْن/الحَزَن», «العَدَم/العُدْم» and «البُخْل/البَخَل»; on this is the poet's saying:
290 - 2- فليتَ زياداً كان في بَطْنِ أمِّه ... وليت زياداً كان وُلْدَ حمارِ
(Would that Ziyād had stayed in his mother's belly; would that Ziyād had been the offspring of a donkey.)
It has been read so in Maryam, al-Zukhruf and Nūḥ among the Seven, as will come, Allah the Exalted willing. «يومَ» is accusative by «اغفر».
[Translator's note: in the second interpretation the source has «وأنْ يكونَ» without an explicit "second"; and «وسكون الياء» presumably refers to the lām (i.e. «وُلْدي»); translated as written.]

semin-durr:42-42.t: The words of Allah the Exalted: {لِيَوْمٍ}, i.e. for the sake of a day; so the lām is causal. It has been said: it means «إلى», i.e. for the limit. The generality read «يُؤَخِّرُهم» with the yāʾ, because the noble name of Allah preceded. Al-Ḥasan, al-Sulamī, al-Aʿraj and many others — and it is related from Abū ʿAmr — read «نُؤَخِّرُهم» with the nūn of majesty. «تَشْخَصُ» is an attribute of «يوم». The meaning of «شُخُوص البصر» is the sharpness of the gaze and its not resting in its place. One says «شَخَص سَهْمُهُ وبَصَرُه» (his arrow / his gaze rose) and «أشخصَهما صاحبُهما» (their owner raised them); «شَخَصَ بصرُه»: his eyelid did not blink. One says «شَخَص مِنْ بلدِه», i.e. he went far away. «الشَّخْص» is the dark form of a person seen from afar.

semin-durr:43-43.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {مُهْطِعِينَ مُقْنِعِي رُءُوسِهِمْ}: two ḥāls (circumstantials) from the omitted muḍāf, since the implied form is "the owners of the eyes", because one says «شَخَصَ زيدٌ بصرَه»; or the eyes indicate their owners, so the ḥāl came from what is indicated. Abū al-Baqāʾ said both of these. It has been said: «مُهْطِعين» is accusative by an implied verb, i.e. "He sees them hastening". «مُقْنِعي» may be a ḥāl from the pronoun in «مُهْطِعين», so that it is an overlapping (mutadākhila) ḥāl. The construct of «مُقْنعي» is not a genuine one, which is why it occurs as a ḥāl.

«الإِهطاع»: it has been said to be hastening in walking. The poet said:
290 - 3- إذا دعانا فأَهْطَعْنا لدَعْوَته ... داعٍ سميعٌ فَلَفُّونا وساقُوْنا
(When a caller, one who is heard, called us and we hastened to his call, they gathered us up and drove us on.)
And another said:
290 - 4- وبمُهْطِعٍ سُرُحٍ كأن عِنَانَه ... في [رأس] جَذْعٍ. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(And on a swift, hastening [horse], as though its rein were on [the top of] a palm trunk …)
Abū ʿUbayda said: "It may be hastening and keeping the gaze fixed." Al-Rāghib said: "«هَطَع الرجلُ ببصره» is when he directs it downward, and «بعيرٌ مُهْطِعٌ» is a camel that lowers its neck." Al-Akhfash said: "It is turning attentively to listening," and he cited:
290 - 5- بِدِجْلَةَ دارُهُمْ ولقد أراهُمْ ... بِدِجْلِةَ مُهْطِعِيْن إلى السَّماعِ
(Their abode is by the Tigris, and I indeed see them by the Tigris, intent upon listening.)
The meaning: turning their heads toward hearing the caller. Thaʿlab said: "«أَهْطَعَ الرجلُ» is when he looks in humiliation and submission, not withdrawing his gaze." This agrees with the statement of Abū ʿUbayd [Translator's note: earlier the source names Abū ʿUbayda]; «أَهْطَعَ» and «هَطَعَ», quadriliteral and triliteral, have both been heard.

«الإِقناع» is raising the head and keeping the gaze fixed without turning to anything else — said by al-Qutabī and Ibn ʿArafa. From it is the saying of the poet describing camels that graze on the tops of trees and so raise their heads:
290 - 6- يُباكِرْن العِضَاهَ بمُقْنَعاتٍ ... نواجِذُهُنَّ كالِحَدأ الوَقيع
(They come early to the thorn-trees with raised [heads], their molars like sharpened axe-heads.)
One also says «أَقْنَعَ رأسَه», i.e. he lowered and bowed it, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings. «القَناعَة» is being content with little; the meaning of «قَنِع بكذا» is that his head is raised above asking. «فَمٌ مُقَنَّع» is a mouth whose teeth are bent inward; and «رجلٌ مُقَنَّعٌ» with doubling. One says «قَنِعَ يَقْنَعُ قَناعةً وقَنَعاً» when he is content, and «قَنَعَ قُنُوعاً» when he begs; so the difference falls in the maṣdar.

Al-Rāghib said: "Some said: the origin of this word is from «القِناع», which is what covers the head. «القانِع» is one who does [not] press in asking and is content with what comes to him, as in the saying:
290 - 7- لَمالُ المَرْءِ يُصْلِحُهُ فَيُغْني ... مَفاقِرَه أعفُّ مِنَ القُنُوعِ
(A man's wealth, which he tends so that it relieves his needs, is more chaste than begging.)
And «رجل مَقْنَعٌ» is one with whom one is satisfied. The poet said:
290 - 8-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... شُهودِيْ على لَيْلَى عُدُولٌ مَقانِعُ
(… my witnesses concerning Laylā are upright, acceptable.)"

«الرُّؤوس» is the plural of «رَأْس», which is feminine [Translator's note: so in the source («مؤنث»); «رأس» is normally treated as masculine]. Its plural of paucity is «أَرْؤُس» and of multitude «رُؤوس». «الأَرْأَس» is one with a large head; it is used to denote a great man, like «الوجه»; «الرئيس» is derived from that; «رِئاس السيف» is its hilt; and «شاةٌ رَأْساء» is a ewe whose head is black.

His words: {لاَ يَرْتَدُّ إِلَيْهِمْ}: also in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun in «مُقْنِعِي». It may be a badal (substitute) from «مُقْنِعي» — so said Abū al-Baqāʾ, meaning that it takes its place. It may also be resumptive.

«الطَّرْف» is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun), and was applied to the agent, as in their saying "There is not among them an eye that blinks"; [perhaps] here it is the eye. The poet said:
290 - 9- وأَغُضُّ طَرْفي ما بَدَتْ لي جارَتي ... حتى يُواري جارَتي مَأْواها
(I lower my gaze whenever my neighbour-woman appears to me, until her dwelling conceals her.)
«الطَّرْف» is also the eyelid; one says "he did not close his «طَرْف» — i.e. his eyelid — upon the other"; and «الطَّرْف» is also the moving of the eyelid.

His words: {وَأَفْئِدَتُهُمْ هَوَآءٌ}: it may be resumptive, or a ḥāl, the governor being either «يَرْتَدُّ» or the governing elements before it. «هواء» is singular though it is the khabar (predicate) of a plural, because it means "empty, torn open"; had that not been intended, He would have said «أَهْوِيَة», so that the khabar agrees with its mubtadaʾ (subject).

«الهواء» is what is empty of bodies, and it is used to denote cowardice; one says «جَوْفُه هواءٌ», i.e. empty. Zuhayr said:
291 - 0- كأن الرَّحْلَ منها فوق صَعْلٍ ... من الظَّلْمَانِ جُؤْجُؤُه هَواءُ
(As though the saddle on her were upon a small-headed male ostrich, whose breast is hollow.)
And Ḥassān ibn Thābit, may Allah be pleased with him, said:
291 - 1-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وأنت مُجَوَّفٌ نَخِبٌ هواءُ
(… while you are hollow, heartless, empty.)
«النَّخِب» is one whose «نُخْبة», i.e. best part, has been taken.

semin-durr:44-44.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمُ}: the second object of «أَنْذِرْ», that is: "frighten them with the punishment of a day." Thus Abū l-Baqāʾ implied it, but there is something to consider in it, since it comes down to your saying "warn of the punishment of the day on which the punishment comes to them," so there is no need for that. Nor is it permissible for it to be an adverbial (ẓarf) of it, because there is no warning on that day, whether it is said that it is the Day of Resurrection, or a day of their destruction, or the day the angels meet them. His saying «نُجِبْ» is the answer to the imperative.
His saying: {أَوَلَمْ تكونوا}: al-Zamakhsharī said: "On the intention of an implied saying, and there are two aspects to it: that they say that out of arrogance and insolence, or that they say it in the tongue of their condition, since they built strongly and hoped far."
And «مالكم» is the answer to the oath. It came in the form of address only because of His saying «أَقْسَمْتُمْ»; had it come in the form of those who swear, it would have been said: "ما لنا." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] implied that saying as being from the words of Allah the Exalted or of the angels, that is: "So it will be said to them: أو لم تكونوا." In my view this is more apparent than the first, I mean the saying proceeding from others, not from them.

semin-durr:45-45.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَسَكَنتُمْ فِي مساكن}: the original usage of «سَكَن» is to be transitive by means of «في», as in this verse, and at times it is transitive by itself. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Sukná is from sukūn, which is lingering (labth), and the original of its transitivity is with «في», as in your saying: «قَرَّ في الدارِ» (he stayed in the house), «أقامَ فيها» (he resided in it), and «غَنِيَ فيها» (he dwelt in it). But when it was transferred to a specific sukūn, it was treated freely, so it was said «سَكَنَ الدارَ» just as it was said «تبوَّأَها» and «أَوْطَنها»; and it is possible that it is from sukūn in the sense of calm, that is: they settled in it and were at ease."
His saying: «وتَبَيَّنَ»: its agent (fāʿil) is a latent pronoun, indicated by the context, [that is]: their condition, their affair and their destruction. And «كيف» is accusative (manṣūb) by «فَعَلْنا»; the interrogative clause is not governed by «تَبَيَّن», because it is one of the verbs that are not suspended (lā tuʿallaq). Nor is it permissible for «كيف» to be the agent, because it is either conditional or interrogative, and neither of the two is governed by what precedes it, and the agent does not come first according to us.
Some of the Kufans said: "The clause «كيف فَعَلْنا» is itself the agent," and they permit a clause to be an agent; this was mentioned shortly before, in His saying, the Exalted: {ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُمْ مِّن بَعْدِ مَا رَأَوُاْ الآيات لَيَسْجُنُنَّهُ} [Yūsuf: 35].
The majority read «تَبَيَّن» as a past verb. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and al-Sulamī, in one report from him, read: «ونُبَيِّنَ» with ḍamma on the first nūn and the second, an imperfect of «بَيَّن»; it is the predicate of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), and the clause is a ḥāl (circumstantial), that is: «ونحنُ نبيِّن». And al-Sulamī read, according to what al-Mahdawī reported, likewise, except that he made the nūn sākin for the jussive, as a conjunction (nasaq) on «تكونوا», so it falls within the scope of the implied saying.
[Translator's note: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb" renders the source's «عمر لن الخطاب», which is evidently a typographical corruption of «عمر بن الخطاب».]

semin-durr:46-46.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَعِندَ الله مَكْرُهُمْ}: it is possible that this maṣdar (verbal noun) is annexed to its agent, like the first, meaning: that their scheming which they schemed, its recompense is with Allah the Exalted; or to the object, meaning: that with Allah is their scheming, which He schemes against them, that is: He punishes them. Al-Zamakhsharī stated both. The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "This is not sound unless «مَكَرَ» is transitive by itself, as he said, since he implied «يمكرهم به»; but what is preserved is that «مَكَر» is not transitive to a direct object by itself. The Exalted said: {وَإِذْ يَمْكُرُ بِكَ الذين كَفَرُواْ} [al-Anfāl: 30], and you say «زيدٌ ممكورٌ به», and «زيدٌ ممكورٌ» is not preserved without the cause."
His saying «لِتَزُولَ»: the majority read it with kasra on the lām, and al-Kisāʾī read it with fatḥa. As for the first reading, it has three aspects. The first: that «إنْ» is negative and the lām is the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd), because it comes after a negated kawn. In «كان» there are then two views. The first: that it is complete (tāmma), and the meaning is belittling their scheming: that it was not such that the laws, which are like mountains in their steadfastness and strength, would pass away through it. What supports its being negative is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd]: «وما كان مَكْرُهم». The second view: that it is incomplete (nāqiṣa), and regarding its predicate there are the two well-known views between the Basrans and the Kufans: is it omitted, with the lām attached to it, which is the position of the Basrans, or is it this lām and what it governs in the genitive, which is the position of the Kufans; this was settled at the end of Āl ʿImrān.
The second aspect: that it is the lightened form of the heavy («إنْ» for «إنَّ»). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Even if their scheming was great and extreme in its severity, so that the passing away of the mountains from it was given as a parable of its severity, that is: even if their scheming was prepared for that." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is possible, in my view, that the meaning of this reading is magnifying their scheming, that is: even if it is severe, it is only done so that great matters would go away by it." The implication of these two statements is that it is the lightened form, because it is an affirmation.
The third: that it is conditional, and its answer is omitted, that is: "even if their scheming was prepared to remove the like of the firm mountains, which are the miracles and the signs, then Allah will requite them with a scheme greater than it." The last two aspects have been preferred over the first, which is that it is negative, because the latter conflicts with the reading of al-Kisāʾī, since his reading announces affirmation, while the reading of others announces negation.
Some of them answered that by saying that the situation in the reading of al-Kisāʾī is an allusion to great matters other than Islam and its miracles, as their scheming had the capacity to remove them, whereas in the reading of the community it is an allusion to what the Prophet ﷺ brought of the true religion, so there is no conflict, as they did not converge on one meaning in negation and affirmation.
As for the reading of al-Kisāʾī, in «إنْ» there are two aspects: the position of the Basrans, that it is the lightened form and the lām is the distinguishing lām (fāriqa); and the position of the Kufans, that it is negative and the lām is in the sense of «إلا». Both positions have been verified earlier.
ʿUmar, ʿAlī, ʿAbd Allāh, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Abū Salama and a group read «وإن كاد مكرهم لَتزول», like the reading of al-Kisāʾī, except that they put a dāl in place of the nūn of «كان», a verb of approximation (fiʿl muqāraba); its analysis is as before, but the passing away does not occur.
And «لَتَزُوْل» was read with fatḥa on both lāms. Its analysis, despite its difficulty, is that it came on the dialect of those who put fatḥa on the lām of «kay».

semin-durr:47-47.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {مُخْلِفَ وَعْدِهِ}: the majority annex «مُخْلِف» to «وعدِه», and there are two aspects to it. The more apparent: that «مُخْلف» is transitive to two objects like its verb, so he put the second object first, and the active participle was annexed to it for lightness, as in «هذا كاسِيْ جُبَّةٍ زيداً» ("this one clothes Zayd with a cloak"). Al-Farrāʾ and Quṭrub said: "Since it is transitive to both of them, no heed is paid to putting one first or last." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: why was it not said «مُخْلِفَ رسلِه وعدَه», and why did He put the second object before the first? I say: He put the promise first to make known that He never breaks the promise; then He said «رسله» to announce that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and breaking promises is not His way, how could He break it to His messengers?"
Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "It is close to their saying:
291 - 2- يا سارقَ الليلةِ أهلَ الدارِ (O thief of the night, of the people of the house)
and some of them recited, as a parallel to the noble verse, the saying of the poet:
291 - 3- ترى الثورَ فيها مُدخِلَ الظلِ رأسَهُ ... وسائرُه بادٍ إلى الشمسِ أجمعُ (You see the bull in it putting its head in the shade, while the rest of it is exposed to the sun, all of it)
and ḥusbān here is: the negated matter, as in his saying:
291 - 4- فلا تَحسَبَنْ أني أَضِلُّ مَنِيَّتي ... فكلُّ امرِئٍ كأسَ الحِمام يذوقُ (Do not think that I miss my fate, for every man will taste the cup of death)
The second: that it is transitive to one, which is «وعدِه», while «رُسُلَه» is accusative by the maṣdar, for it resolves into a maṣdar particle and a verb, its implied form being: «مُخْلِفُ ما وعدَ رُسُلَه», where «ما» is maṣdar-forming, not in the sense of «alladhī»."
[Translator's note: the passage from "Abū l-Baqāʾ said" onward is garbled in the source: the quotation marks are not closed, the verse numbering (291-2 to 291-4) is interleaved with the text, and the line "ثانٍ" at the start of the second aspect ("الثاني") is run on with the end of verse 291-4. I have translated what is written, keeping the verse numbers; the second verse's gloss and the attribution of the wording after the verses are as they appear in the source.]
A group read {مُخْلِفَ وَعْدَ رُسُلَهُ} with accusative on «وعدَه» and genitive on «رسله», separating the two annexed terms by the object. It is like the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir {قَتْلُ أَوْلاَدَهمْ شُرَكَآئِهِمْ}; al-Zamakhsharī said, boldly: "And this is as weak as the one who read {قَتْلُ أَوْلاَدَهمْ شُرَكَآئِهِمْ}."

semin-durr:48-48.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {يَوْمَ تُبَدَّلُ}: several aspects are permissible in it. The first: that it is accusative (manṣūb) by «انتقام», that is: His vengeance takes place on that day. The second: that it is accusative by «اذكْر» (remember). The third: that it is accusative by what is distilled from the meaning of {عَزِيزٌ ذُو انتقام}. The fourth: that it is a badal (substitute) of {يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمُ} [Ibrāhīm: 44]. The fifth: that it is accusative by «مُخْلِف». The sixth: that it is accusative by «وَعْدِه», with «إنَّ» and what follows it being a parenthetical clause. Abū l-Baqāʾ ruled out these last two, saying: "because what precedes «inna» does not govern what follows it." That is not a barrier, because, as was said, it is a parenthetical clause, so no heed is paid to it as a separator.
His saying «والسماواتُ»: its implied form is: «وتُبَدَّل السماواتُ غيرَ السماواتِ» (and the heavens will be changed into other than the heavens). Regarding the changing there are two views: is it connected with the essence or with the attribute? Ibn ʿAbbās inclined to the second, and he recited:
291 - 5- فما الناسُ بالناسِ الذين عَهِدْتُهُمْ ... ولا الدارُ التي كنتُ تَعْلَمُ (The people are not the people whom I knew, nor is the abode the one you used to know)
And «نُبَدِّل» was read with nūn, with «الأرضَ» accusative and «السماواتِ» conjoined (nasaq) to it.
His saying: «وبَرَزوا»: there are two aspects to it. One: that it is a resumptive clause, that is: «ويَبْرُزُون» (and they will come forth); so Abū l-Baqāʾ implied it, meaning that it is a past verb intended for the future. The better view is that it is like {ونادى أَصْحَابُ النار} [al-Aʿrāf: 50], {ونادى أَصْحَابُ الجنة} [al-Aʿrāf: 44], {رُّبَمَا يَوَدُّ الذين كَفَرُواْ} [al-Ḥijr: 2], {أتى أَمْرُ الله} [al-Naḥl: 1], because of the certainty of that.
The second: that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «الأرض», with «قد» intended with it; Abū l-Baqāʾ said it. The pronoun in «بَرَزوا» would then refer to creation, which the context indicates, and the link between the ḥāl and its owner is the wāw.
Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «وبُرِّزوا» with ḍamma on the bāʾ and kasra on the rāʾ, doubled, to indicate intensification in the verb and its object.

semin-durr:49-49.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {مُّقَرَّنِينَ}: it may be a ḥāl (circumstantial), if the verb is one of sight, and it may be a second object, if the verb is one of knowledge. And {فِي الأصفاد} is attached to it. It was also said: to an omitted element, as a ḥāl or an adjective of «مُقَرَّنين». The muqarran is the one gathered in the qaran, which is the rope with which one is tied. He [the poet] said:
291 - 6- وابنُ اللَّبونِ إذا ما لُزَّ في قَرَنٍ ... لم يَسْتَطِعْ صَوْلَةَ البُزْلِ القَناعِيٍسِ (The young camel, when it is bound in a rope, cannot withstand the charge of the strong, mighty camels)
And another said:
291 - 7- والخيرُ والشرُّ مَلْزُوْزان في قَرَنْ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (Good and evil are bound together in a rope ...)
In the exegesis: every disbeliever is bound together with his devil in a chain.
And al-aṣfād: the plural of ṣafad, which is the shackle and the fetter. It is said: «صَفَده يَصْفِدُه صَفْداً» (he fettered him); the noun is al-ṣafad, and «صَفَّده», doubled, is for intensification. He [the poet] said:
298 - 1- فآبُوا بالنهَّائِبِ والسَّبايا ... وأُبْنا بالمُلوكِ مُصفَّدينا (They returned with the plunder and the captives, and we returned with the kings fettered)
[Translator's note: the verse number appears in the source as 298 - 1, though the sequence of the surrounding numbers (291 - 7, 291 - 9) suggests 291 - 8; I have kept the number as written.]
And al-ṣifād is like al-ṣafad, and «أَصْفَده» means: he gave him. So they distinguished between faʿala and afʿala. It was also said: rather, both are used for fettering and for giving.
Al-Nābigha said:
291 - 9- . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ...
فلم أُعَرِّض -أبيتَ اللَّعْنَ- بالصَّفَد (so I did not allude — may you refuse curses — to the giving)
that is: to the giving. Giving was called ṣafad because it binds the one to whom it is given; and from it comes "I am shackled by your favours and a captive of your bounty."

semin-durr:50-50.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {سَرَابِيلُهُم مِّن قَطِرَانٍ}: mubtadaʾ and khabar (subject and predicate) in the position of accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial): either from «المجرمين», or from «مُقَرَّنين», or from its pronoun. It may also be resumptive, and this is the apparent view.
Al-sarābīl: garments. «سَرْبَلْتُه» means: you clothed him with the sirbāl. He [the poet] said:
292 - 0- أَوْدَى بنَعْلَيَّ وسِرْباليَهْ (It destroyed my two sandals and my two garments)
and it is applied to what fortifies in war, such as armour and the like. The Exalted said: {وَسَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُم بَأْسَكُمْ} [al-Naḥl: 81].
Al-qaṭirān: what is extracted from a tree, then boiled and smeared on mangy camels so that their mange goes away by its sharpness; and it is the best of things for kindling with. There are dialects in it: qaṭirān with fatḥa on the qāf and kasra on the ṭāʾ, which is the reading of the majority. Qaṭrān on the pattern of sakrān, with which ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib read. Abū l-Najm said:
292 - 1- لَبَّسَه القَطْرانَ والمُسُوحَا ... (He clothed him in tar and in coarse haircloth)
And qiṭrān with kasra on the qāf and sukūn on the ṭāʾ, on the pattern of sirḥān; it was not read so, as far as I know.
A large group, among them ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra and al-Ḥasan, read «بَقَطِرٍ آنٍ» with fatḥa on the qāf, kasra on the ṭāʾ and tanwīn on the rāʾ, and «آنٍ» on the pattern of ʿānin, making them two words. Al-qaṭir is copper, and al-ānī is an active participle of «أَنَى يَأْني», that is: it reached the utmost in heat, as in His saying: {وَبَيْنَ حَمِيمٍ آنٍ} [al-Raḥmān: 44]. And from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is not the tar, but rather the copper that takes on its colour."
And «وتَغَشَّى» was read with doubled shīn, that is «وتَتَغشَّى», with one of the two tāʾs omitted.
It was also read with «وجوهُهم» nominative and «النار» accusative, by way of figurative speech, making the faces' coming to the Fire a covering.
As for the clause «وتَغْشى», Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "also a ḥāl," meaning that it is conjoined to the ḥāl, and he does not mean that it is a ḥāl with the wāw being a wāw of the ḥāl, because it is an affirmative imperfect.

semin-durr:51-51.t: His saying, the Exalted: {لِيَجْزِيَ}: in this verse there are two aspects. The better of them: that it is attached to «بَرَزُوا», and on this view His saying «وَتَرَى» is a parenthetical clause between the attached element and that to which it is attached. The second: that it is attached to an omitted element, that is: "We did that to the criminals so that He might recompense every soul"; because when He punishes the criminal, He rewards the obedient.

semin-durr:52-52.t:
And His saying, the Exalted: {هذا} is a pointer to what precedes, from His saying {فَلاَ تَحْسَبَنَّ} [Ibrāhīm: 47] up to here, or to the whole Qurʾān, which is treated as though present.
His saying: «وَلِيُنْذَروا»: there are several aspects in it. The first: that it is attached to an omitted element, that is: «وليُنْذِرُوا به أَنْزَلْنا عليك» (We sent it down to you so that they may be warned by it).
The second: that it is conjoined to an omitted element, and that omitted element is attached to «بلاغ», its implied form being: «ليُنْصَحوا ولِيُنْذَروا» (so that they may be advised and warned). The third: that the wāw is redundant (zāʾida) and «لِيُنْذَروا» is attached to «بلاغ»; this is the opinion of al-Akhfash, reported by al-Māwardī. The fourth: that it is construed according to the meaning, that is: «ليُبَلَّغُوا ولِيُنْذَرُوا» (so that it be conveyed to them and they be warned). The fifth: that the lām is the lām of command. Some of them said: it is good were it not for His saying «ولِيَذَّكَّر», which is only accusative. I say: there is no objection in that, for His saying «ولِيَذَّكَّرَ» is not conjoined to what precedes it, but is attached to an implied verb, that is: «ولِيَذَّكَّر أَنْزَلْناه وأَوْحيناه» (We sent it down and revealed it so that he may take heed). The sixth: that it is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject). The implied form: «هذا بلاغٌ وهو ليذَّكَّر»; Ibn ʿAṭiyya said it. The seventh: that it is the conjunction of a singular to a singular, that is: "this is a delivery of the message and a warning"; al-Mubarrad said it, and it is an explanation of meaning, not of i'rab.
The eighth: that it is conjoined to His saying {لِتُخْرِجَ الناس} [Ibrāhīm: 1] at the beginning of the sūra. This is very strange. The ninth: Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "The meaning: this is a delivery of the message to the people and for the warning, so it is attached to «بلاغ» or to an omitted element if you make «الناس» an adjective; and it may be attached to an omitted element, its implied form being: «ولِيُنْذَروا به أُنْزِل وتُلِي» (it was sent down and recited so that they may be warned by it)." I say: the implication leads to the construction remaining: "this is a delivery of the message for the warning," and the warning cannot be a purpose of that.
The majority read «لِيُنْذَرُوا» as a passive. Mujāhid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays read «ولِتُنْذِرُوا» with a ḍamma-vowelled tāʾ and kasra on the dhāl, as though the delivery is for everyone and the warning is for those addressed.
Yaḥyā ibn ʿUmāra al-Dhāriʿ, from his father, and Aḥmad ibn Yazīd ibn Usayd al-Sulamī read «ولِيُنْذَرُوا» with fatḥa on the yāʾ and the dhāl, from «نَذَر بالشيء», that is: he knew of it and so prepared for it. They said: no maṣdar is known for it, so it is like «ʿasā» and other verbs that have no verbal nouns.
